lesson.title: Wann genau? jetzt, sofort, später, früh, endlich
lesson.subtitle: point-in-time adverbs — German's five answers to 'when exactly?'

hook.title: When Exactly — Without a Preposition
hook.content: English answers 'when' with a noun: at noon, in the morning, at once. German has five adverbs that answer it with nothing but a word. jetzt (now), sofort (at once — never 'soon', a trap for anyone who pattern-matches on soon), später (later), früh (early — one f, and it never means 'too early'), endlich (finally / at last). All five drop into the same slot behind the conjugated verb that immer and oft just used, which means the frequency lesson and the time lesson are the same lesson wearing different vocabulary. Two of them travel: Bis später! is one of the three most common farewells in the language, and Endlich ist der Sommer da is the sentence you say when a wait finally ends.

footnotes.title: sofort Is Not soon
footnotes.content: Komm bitte sofort! means 'come right now', urgently — the adverb sits closer to at once than to soon. If you want 'soon', German reaches for bald (from topic 8) or a gar bald: Bald bin ich da.

pattern.title: Same Slot, Five Words
pattern.content: The frame never changes: verb in slot 2, time adverb behind it, everything else follows. Jetzt lerne ich Deutsch (now I am learning German). Der Zug fährt sehr früh (the train leaves very early). Endlich ist der Sommer da (at last summer is here). With a separable verb the adverb can also be pushed to the very front — Endlich kommt er (at last he is coming) — because an adverb in position 1 does exactly what a negated verb or a conjunction does. And the farewell: Bis später! takes the accusative of time you already own.
pattern.linguist_note: English made temporal 'when' a preposition word (at, in, on) and then fed it nouns. German kept the adverb slot empty and let single words fill it — which is why German sentences carry time as a flat adverb where English carries a small prepositional phrase.

exercises.prompt: Point in time — match each sentence with its reading:
exercises.target_answer: Jetzt lerne ich Deutsch, Der Zug fährt sehr früh, Endlich ist der Sommer da, Komm bitte sofort mit, Bis später
exercises.meaning: now, early, finally, at once, later
exercises.explanation: No preposition anywhere. The adverb goes behind the conjugated verb — or takes position 1 and pushes the verb to slot 2 (Jetzt lerne ich).

exercises.prompt: 'Komm bitte _____!' (Come here AT ONCE, please) — which word means 'at once', not 'soon'?
exercises.meaning: Komm bitte sofort! = come here right now
exercises.explanation: sofort sits on the at-once end of the line. bald is the 'soon' of topic 8, später is later, früh is early. English soon has no single German twin.

exercises.prompt: Adverb to position 1: '_____ kommt er.' (At last he is coming):
exercises.meaning: Endlich kommt er = at last he is coming
exercises.explanation: An adverb in position 1 does what a negated verb does: kommt slides to slot 2. Same swap as Jetzt lerne ich Deutsch.

exercises.prompt: 'Der Zug fährt sehr früh' — the verb behind fährt has a living English twin. Which?
exercises.meaning: fahren ↔ fare: the same old go-verb, alive in wayfarer and seafarer
exercises.explanation: fahren is English fare's twin — the same ancient go-verb that survives in wayfarer and seafarer (der Fahrer is the one who fares). früh, for honesty's sake, has no twin at all: English lost that word, and the German cousin of English early lives in the ere-family as eher.

vocab_hints.note: one f, long ü. Der Zug fährt früh — the adverb rides behind the conjugated verb fährt, exactly like immer and oft did.

exercises.explanation: fahren in slot 2 (Der takes slot 1), then the adverb. Note the contrast pair waiting in the bank: spät is 'late', früh is 'early' — the same train, two hours apart.
cues: Opens with "Der Zug" and ends with "früh".

summary.outcome: Answer 'when exactly?' with one adverb, in the slot behind the verb.

use_example.german: Jetzt lerne ich Deutsch — bis später!
use_example.english: Now I am learning German — see you later!

summary.takeaway: jetzt, sofort, später, früh, endlich — five time adverbs, no preposition, same slot as immer and oft. sofort is at once, not soon.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the calendar itself — Januar bis Mai, the Latin months with German mouths.

jetzt.etymology_derivation: Old High German iozuo, je (ever) + zu (to); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

sofort.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Middle Low German so vōrt — literally 'so forth', mirroring the English phrase. [wiktionary]

später.etymology_derivation: Comparative of spät (late); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

früh.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *frō(ī); only Dutch/Low German cognates listed. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

endlich.etymology_derivation: Ende + -lich, a formation the page itself compares to English endly; Ende is the documented twin of end. [wiktionary]

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

olive.context_phrase: Die Pizza mit Oliven schmeckt gut.
olive.context_translation: The pizza with olives tastes good.
olive.etymology_derivation: From Latin oliva, partly through Middle High German olive; English olive is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]

breit.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braidaz — the exact twin of English broad (Old English brād), with German breit named as its cognate by etymonline. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

ratte.context_phrase: Eine Ratte läuft durch den Keller.
ratte.context_translation: A rat runs through the cellar.
ratte.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ratta, from Proto-West Germanic *ratt, from Proto-Germanic *rattaz. English rat is the cognate. [wiktionary]

sekretärin.etymology_derivation: Sekretär (secretary) + -in; Sekretär is borrowed from Latin secretarius (keeper of secrets) - the same Latin word as English secretary. [wiktionary][etymonline]

fremder.context_phrase: Der Fremde fragt nach dem Weg.
fremder.context_translation: The stranger asks for the way.
fremder.etymology_derivation: fremd + -er; the dictionary documents fremd as the twin of the obsolete English word fremd, foreign — a stranger, a foreigner to you. [wiktionary]
